summary: This deck explains how frugal innovations are developed by treating constraints in emerging markets as the starting point for design rather than as obstacles. It presents a structured approach that identifies constraints, uses root cause analysis to uncover underlying problems, converts them into product requirements, and iteratively develops a frugal MVP. Case studies including GE Lullaby Warmer and iBreastExam illustrate how low-cost, robust, user-friendly solutions emerge from this process.

Constraint-Based Thinking: A Structured Approach for Developing Frugal Innovations
A constraint is anything that limits the performance of a system.
A constraint is anything that limits the performance or freedom of a system.
Examples: Only 5000/- available for a project. Only two engineers in a team. No internet connectivity. Limited power supply.  Limited manufacturing equipment. How to solve?
Every engineering project has some constraints.
Innovation does not continuously increase with constraints. Instead, it follows an Inverted U curve.
A. Limiting Constraints: These reduce creativity.
Examples: Excessive time pressure, Too many regulations
B. Channeling Constraints: These actually improve innovation.
Examples: Budget limit, Weight limit, Power consumption limit , Maximum product cost, Clear design requirements
Table provides a brief overview of several decades’ study evaluating the influence of constraints on innovation and creativity
Positive | Time pressure improved usefulness, innovation, and productivity. | A moderate deadline motivates people to focus and work efficiently.
Negative | Too much time pressure reduced innovation and productivity. | Excessive deadlines create stress, reducing creativity.
Ambivalent | Constraints differ for small and large organizations. | The same constraint has different effects depending on the organization.

Ambivalent | Inverted U-shaped relationship between time pressure and creativity. | Too little pressure - people procrastinate. Moderate pressure - highest creativity. Too much pressure - creativity declines.
Ambivalent | Context determines whether constraints help or hurt. | The environment matters. The same constraint may be useful in one situation but harmful in another.
Ambivalent | Product and process constraints affect creativity differently. | Different constraints influence different parts of innovation.
Positive | Design constraints stimulate creativity. | Working within clear limits encourages creative thinking.
Negative | Bureaucratic barriers hinder innovation. | Too many approvals slow down progress.
Negative | Financial, market, and regulatory constraints can inhibit innovation. | Lack of funding or strict regulations can stop promising ideas.
Positive | Moderate constraints foster innovation. | Innovation is highest when constraints are balanced, not too few and not too many.
Negative | Too few constraints cause complacency; too many reduce motivation. | Unlimited resources reduce urgency, while excessive restrictions frustrate teams.
Frugal innovation does not eliminate constraints. It uses constraints as a design challenge.
OneDollarGlasses, M-Pesa mobile banking, ChotuKool refrigerators, Haier washing machines for clothes and vegetables, and PeekVision eye diagnostics are examples of such frugal innovations
Root Cause Analysis:  Understand the real reason behind each constraint.
Process of repeatedly asking "Why did this happen?" until the fundamental cause of a problem is identified, allowing a permanent solution rather than a temporary fix.
Problem: Students scored poorly in the exam.
Why? → They could not answer application based questions.
Why? → They memorized concepts instead of understanding.
Why? → Teaching focused theory rather than problem solving.
Why? → Few practical examples and activities were included.
Root Cause:Teaching approach focused on memorization rather than conceptual learning.
Solution:Include case studies, hands-on activities, and problem-based learning.
Problem: Farmers waste large amounts of water.
Why 2?→ Farmers don't know the soil moisture level.
Why 5?→ Technologies are designed for large farms.
Root Cause:❖ Affordable sensing technology is unavailable.
Problem: Phone battery lasts only a few hours.
Why 1?→ Too many apps run continuously.
Why 2?→ Background processes are always active.
Why 5?→ Users are unaware of power-saving settings.
Root Cause:❖ Poor battery management and user awareness.

In reality, one problem usually has multiple root causes, not a single one. RCA is about identifying all significant causes, then deciding which ones to address first. This is especially important in frugal innovation.
Problem: Low Vaccination Rate in a Village
Parents are unaware of vaccine schedules.
Clinic timings conflict with work hours.
RCA Conclusion:The problem is caused by multiple factors, not just one.
Instead of building a new hospital (high cost), several low-cost solutions address the major root causes.

Constraint-based thinking problem and solution space
Problem Space ("Why?") identifies the real-world challenges and constraints.
Solution Space ("What?") translates those constraints into product features.
Constraint-based thinking prevents overengineering by focusing only on essential requirements.
Process is iterative, moving back and forth between understanding the problem and refining solution until frugal product is achieved.
Constraints are not obstacles; they are the driving force behind frugal innovation.
Traditional innovation often begins with available technology, new features, market competition; Frugal innovation begins with Constraints, Resource limitations and Unmet needs.
